digests.narrative:
Photonics is the theme he owns hardest, and the argument is unchanged: as AI networking moves from pluggable modules toward co-packaged optics, indium phosphide laser supply becomes the chokepoint, and very few public companies can fill it. Late July handed him the strongest external validation yet — a $300m US CHIPS award to GlobalFoundries aimed explicitly at silicon photonics and CPO, with Sivers and Lumentum the only two public laser suppliers named in the programme.

The hard evidence sits with Lumentum. Its CEO put the supply-demand gap above 30% in EMLs and pump lasers, record quarterly revenue of $808m was up 90%, and the Japanese wafer fab is fully allocated. AXT's long-term agreement is the corroboration that matters: Lumentum is prepaying deposits totalling $87m to reserve substrate capacity through 2031, which is behaviour, not commentary.

Where the theme is weakest is precisely where he is most invested. Sivers reported Q1 net sales down 22% year on year, and the $799m he cites is an opportunity pipeline rather than backlog. AAOI's $471m-a-month 2027 figure is roughly five times what management guides to. The POET wording change he read as a timeline upgrade still resolves to production readiness by end-2026 — a milestone, not an order.
keyPoints: US CHIPS award to GlobalFoundries names Sivers and Lumentum as the only public laser suppliers in the CPO programme
Lumentum: record $808m revenue up 90%, supply-demand gap above 30%, Japan fab fully allocated
AXT reserves InP capacity for Lumentum through 2031 against $87m of deposits, paid in two tranches
Sivers Q1 net sales fell 22% year on year; the $799m headline is a pipeline, not backlog
AAOI's $471m/month 2027 rate is about five times management's own $1.1bn full-year guide
POET/Sivers language remains production readiness by end-2026, with prototypes in the first half

digests.narrative:
The memory upcycle remains one of his highest-conviction structural calls, and Micron's quarter gave it its strongest evidence yet: record DRAM revenue of $31.3bn, up 343% year on year, at an 84.9% consolidated gross margin, with 16 strategic customer agreements and remaining performance obligations above $5bn. Amazon naming higher memory costs as a driver of its capex increase is the demand side of the same story, visible from the buyer's accounts.

He reads the contracts as a structural change to how memory is sold. The qualification is the coverage: only around 20% of DRAM and 30% of NAND volume sits under those agreements, so roughly four fifths of DRAM volume remains spot-exposed. The contracts smooth the cycle rather than remove it, and they defend floor pricing and volume rather than the pricing above the floor that currently carries the earnings.

Sentiment and price have moved the other way regardless. Memory names sold off hard through late July, and much of his coverage this week was a defence of the framing around that drawdown rather than new evidence about the business.
keyPoints: Micron fiscal Q3 DRAM revenue of $31.3bn, up 343%, at an 84.9% consolidated gross margin
16 strategic customer agreements with remaining performance obligations above $5bn
Only about 20% of DRAM and 30% of NAND volume is contracted — most remains spot-exposed
An 84.9% gross margin reads as a cycle peak rather than a run-rate
Amazon attributed part of its capex increase to higher memory costs
Memory equities fell sharply into the drawdown despite the contractual demand lock

digests.narrative:
The fab layer is where he tracks whether the buildout has manufacturing behind it, and the late-July flow was mostly policy and packaging. The US signed a $300m CHIPS letter of intent with GlobalFoundries for silicon photonics and co-packaged optics R&D, taking roughly 1% equity — federal money pointed directly at his central theme. He was surprised the stock stayed down; $300m against a $27bn company is immaterial, and the market priced it accordingly.

Packaging is the other constraint in view. Nvidia signed a $1.5bn prepaid agreement with Amkor for US advanced packaging capacity, on top of a ten-year TSMC partnership, and FormFactor's call attributed nearly doubled systems revenue to accelerating CPO growth — small absolute numbers, but the first CPO revenue showing up in anyone's accounts.

Intel is the awkward name. Q2 revenue of $16.1bn was up 25%, the strongest growth in over fifteen years, and it still produced a GAAP loss of $2.16 a share. On the disclosed schedule 14A reaches risk production in 2027 and high volume in 2028, so external foundry revenue is not a near-term event.
keyPoints: GlobalFoundries signed a $300m CHIPS letter of intent for silicon photonics and CPO, with Commerce taking about 1%
Nvidia committed $1.5bn in prepayments to Amkor for US advanced packaging capacity
FormFactor attributed near-doubled systems revenue to accelerating co-packaged optics
Intel Q2 revenue $16.1bn, up 25%, yet GAAP EPS was negative $2.16
Intel 14A reaches risk production in 2027 and high volume in 2028
The $300m award is immaterial to GlobalFoundries' scale, which explains the muted price reaction

digests.narrative:
The neocloud thesis is that companies contracting power and capacity ahead of demand convert scarcity into annualised run-rate, and both names he follows delivered on that this period. IREN revised its ARR target above $4bn on new AI cloud contracts naming Microsoft, Nvidia, Perplexity and Figure. Nebius secured up to 1.2GW of power and land for an owned Pennsylvania site and expects more than 3GW under contract by year-end.

What the price action showed was how leveraged these names are to positioning rather than fundamentals. A single large liquidation moved Nebius and IREN more than 25% in a day, which he read correctly as forced selling rather than information.

The risk the theme actually carries is financing, not demand. Nebius reported $399m of quarterly revenue against a $3-3.4bn full-year target, so nearly the entire guide sits in the second half, and capex plans run an order of magnitude above revenue. Contracted ARR is not funded capacity, and the terms of the next raise matter more to the equity than GPU demand does.
keyPoints: IREN revised its ARR target above $4bn with Microsoft, Nvidia, Perplexity and Figure named
Nebius secured up to 1.2GW in Pennsylvania and expects over 3GW contracted by year-end
Nebius Q1 revenue of $399m annualises near $1.6bn against a $3-3.4bn full-year target
Capex plans run an order of magnitude above revenue — this is a financing story first
A single fund liquidation moved both names more than 25% in a day
Nebius reports Q2 on 12 August, the next test of the second-half step-up

digests.narrative:
The materials layer is his answer to the question of what breaks first if the buildout accelerates, and the read this period was that the equipment and test names are already printing the growth the theme predicts. Teradyne reported revenue up 104% with EPS growth above 300%, and Bloom Energy delivered 166% revenue growth with expanding margins and raised guidance — results he used to argue that the July drawdown was indiscriminate deleveraging rather than deteriorating fundamentals.

Aehr remains the specific position. Its 2027 guide of $130-150m implies 160-200% growth and explicitly assumes little or no memory revenue and nothing from a newly benchmarked AI customer, which he reads as a guide with deliberate room above it.

The through-line is that upstream names sell into every downstream winner, so they express the theme without requiring a call on which laser or memory supplier wins. That is also why they fell with everything else in the drawdown despite the results.
keyPoints: Teradyne revenue up 104% with EPS growth above 300%
Bloom Energy revenue up 166% with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance
Aehr guides 2027 to $130-150m, implying 160-200% growth
The Aehr guide assumes little or no memory revenue and nothing from a newly benchmarked AI customer
Strong results across the layer did not prevent the July drawdown, which he reads as deleveraging
Upstream exposure captures the theme without picking the winning downstream supplier

digests.narrative:
Networking sits between his optics thesis and the accelerator roadmaps, and the period's most useful input was a channel check on Chinese laser capability: no working 200G EMLs, and some distance from high-power continuous-wave sources for near-package and co-packaged optics. If that holds, the Western laser supply chain keeps its position through the CPO transition rather than being commoditised.

The AMD event was the scheduled catalyst, with brokers expecting scale-up CPO and MI500 roadmap disclosure. What emerged was executive commentary rather than commitment, which leaves the networking read-through as inference.

Marvell continues to appear only in breadth lists rather than in a dedicated thesis, down about a third on the month with no company-specific claim attached. That pattern — mention volume generated by market moves rather than by analysis — is worth separating from genuine coverage when reading this theme's ranking.
keyPoints: Channel check: Chinese suppliers lack working 200G EMLs and high-power CW sources for NPO and CPO
The AMD event produced CPO commentary rather than a product commitment
Marvell appears only in market-breadth posts, with no dedicated thesis behind the mentions
Substrate tightness is spreading — Samsung reportedly struggling to secure large FC-BGA substrates
Optical networking names led the recovery off the July lows, moving as a single high-beta block

digests.narrative: One clarifying datapoint: CPO hasn't scaled yet, and much of the Corning story rides the 2028 FAU TAM — so the recent CPO delay-report cycle and glass-bridge uncertainty hit exactly where GLW's optics earnings live. His framing stays consistent with the MS recap: the glass bridge has potential in the CPO stack but displacing incumbent FAU solutions near-term is hard. Tracked, not owned; the theme stays a placeholder until CPO volumes actually arrive.
keyPoints: GLW's optics case leans on the 2028 FAU TAM — CPO hasn't scaled yet
CPO delay-report cycle and glass-bridge uncertainty hit the earnings timeline directly
Still no dedicated glass-substrate thesis — tracked, not owned

digests.narrative:
Robotics is his longest-dated theme and the one furthest from revenue. The period's catalyst was a reported FCC move to ban Chinese imports of humanoid and quadruped robots to protect American programmes, which he reads as a direct positive for US players including Agility Robotics. He pairs it with Musk's repeated claim that Optimus will be Tesla's biggest product ever, and with supplier-rate requirements that give the Tesla programme a dated, checkable milestone.

The structural argument is that China ships roughly 90% of the world's humanoids today, so protection plus capital is what an American supply chain needs to exist at all.

The exposure itself needs care. Agility is reached through a pre-close SPAC that values it at roughly $2.5bn with over $620m of gross proceeds, and that only converts after SEC review of the S-4, a shareholder vote and closing expected before end-2026, after which it trades under a different ticker. Deal and redemption risk currently sit above operating risk, and the import-ban read-through is regulatory rather than a statement about the products themselves.
keyPoints: FCC reportedly set to ban Chinese imports of humanoid and quadruped robots
China ships roughly 90% of the world's humanoid robots today
Agility exposure is a pre-close SPAC valuing it at about $2.5bn with over $620m of gross proceeds
The combination still needs S-4 review, a shareholder vote and closing before end-2026
Musk repeated that Optimus will be Tesla's biggest product ever
Tesla supplier requirements give the Optimus ramp a dated, checkable milestone

digests.narrative:
He treats the accelerator layer less as a place to own and more as the clock everything else runs on. Nvidia's quarter confirmed the demand hub is intact — record data centre revenue of $75.2bn, up 92%, with networking revenue close to tripling — and his consistent position is to express the view through the suppliers this map surfaces rather than through Nvidia itself.

The live question is AMD and co-packaged optics. Channel checks after the Advancing AI event pointed to AMD pursuing CPO for future Helios generations, and he reads that as the trigger that converts the laser suppliers from thematic to scheduled. That claim currently has no AMD disclosure behind it: Helios and MI450 ship in the second half of 2026 on pluggable optics, with CPO described as a future-generation option, which places any read-through in 2027 at the earliest.

One counterweight he does not raise. Nvidia returned roughly $20bn to shareholders and authorised $80bn more of buyback in the same quarter its customers raised capex. At a 74.9% gross margin it is the customers' cost line, and the first sign of strain in this system will appear in the payers' earnings.
keyPoints: Nvidia FQ1 data centre revenue of $75.2bn, up 92%, with networking revenue near tripling
AMD data centre revenue up 57% with the next quarter guided to about 46% growth
AMD CPO adoption rests on channel checks and broker notes, not company disclosure
Helios and MI450 ship in H2 2026 on pluggable optics; CPO is a future generation
Nvidia returned about $20bn and authorised $80bn more of buyback while customers raised capex
At 74.9% gross margin Nvidia is the cost line its customers are funding

digests.narrative:
His core macro claim is that the buildout is demand-constrained rather than overbuilt, and the late-July earnings round supported it. Combined 2026 capex guidance across Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft moved to roughly $720-745bn from $695-725bn, and Amazon's CEO said explicitly that even $220bn will not meet 2026 demand, with the same expected in 2027. He contrasts this directly with media framing that hyperscalers had overbuilt and were reselling excess compute.

The distinction the numbers now force is between capex that is funded and capex that is not. Alphabet raised to $195-205bn while cloud revenue grew 82%; Meta raised its floor by $10bn and missed quarterly EPS badly, with the shares falling about 8%. Reading the group as one signal loses that difference.

Two qualifications apply to the read-through he draws for suppliers. Part of the increase is memory cost inflation rather than incremental compute units, and only around 40% of Alphabet's capex goes to data centres and networking rather than servers. The dollars are real; the share that reaches optics and interconnect is smaller than the headline implies.
keyPoints: Combined 2026 capex guidance rose to roughly $720-745bn from $695-725bn
Amazon lifted 2026 capex to $220bn and still expects to be short of capacity in 2026 and 2027
Alphabet raised to $195-205bn with cloud revenue up 82% — the best-funded spend in the group
Meta raised its capex floor $10bn and missed Q2 EPS; the equity derated about 8%
Part of the capex increase is memory cost inflation, not additional compute units
Roughly 40% of Alphabet's capex is data centre and networking, the only slice reaching optics
